engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

chess.title: Calculation: The LPDO Rule
chess.body: LPDO = Loose Pieces Drop Off. Before every move, scan the board: which of my pieces are undefended? Which of my opponent's pieces are undefended? Undefended pieces are targets for tactics. A simple habit: after finding your move, ask 'does this leave anything undefended?' This alone prevents most blunders.

book.author: Cal Newport
book.chapter: The Shallow Work Trap: Why Being Busy Is Not the Same as Being Productive
book.lesson: Shallow work is non-cognitively demanding tasks performed while distracted — email, meetings, admin. Deep work is professional activity performed in a state of distraction-free concentration that pushes your cognitive capabilities to their limit. These efforts create new value, improve your skill, and are hard to replicate. Newport's argument: the ability to do deep work is becoming increasingly rare at exactly the same time it is becoming increasingly valuable in the economy. The few who cultivate this skill will thrive.
book.key_quote: Two to four hours of genuine deep work produces more output than eight hours of fragmented shallow work.
book.action: Schedule one 90-minute deep work block tomorrow. No phone, no email, one hard problem. Treat it like a meeting you cannot cancel.
crux: Deep work: focused, undistracted, cognitively demanding work. It is becoming rare and simultaneously more valuable.
Two core abilities now decide income: learn hard things fast, and produce elite output fast.
Both abilities depend on deep work. Both are destroyed by fragmented attention.
Shallow work is logistically necessary and infinitely replaceable. It feels like work and produces nothing durable.
Attention residue: switching tasks leaves cognitive drag for 15–20 minutes. Ten switches cost you the day.
High-quality work = time spent × intensity of focus. Intensity is the neglected multiplier.
Four scheduling philosophies: monastic, bimodal, rhythmic, journalistic. Rhythmic — same hours daily — is the only one most people can sustain.
Willpower is finite and depletes. Rituals and fixed locations spend none of it.
Schedule every minute of the workday. Not to obey it, but to force the question 'what deserves this hour?'
Fixed-schedule productivity: hard-stop the day and work backwards. Constraint forces ruthless triage.
Boredom tolerance is trainable and prerequisite. If every queue is filled with a phone, focus never develops.
Quit social media by default; readmit a tool only if it clearly serves a core goal.
Drain the shallows. Aim shallow work under 40% of the week and defend the rest.
learnings: Busy is not a proxy for valuable. It is usually a proxy for unfocused.
The ability to concentrate is a skill you build, not a mood you catch.
Fragmented time is not additive — four 30-minute blocks are worth far less than one 2-hour block.
Downtime is not idleness; unconscious processing needs it.
examples: Carl Jung built a stone tower at Bollingen and wrote there in the mornings, uninterrupted, while running a clinical practice.
Adam Grant compressed teaching into one semester and batched research into the other — becoming one of the most published psychologists of his generation.
Newport wrote a book, earned a PhD, and published peer-reviewed papers while rarely working past 5:30pm, by hard-stopping his day.
adapt: One 90-minute block before 8am for the highest-leverage build. Phone in another room, not face-down on the desk.
Batch Telegram, Instagram, and email into two windows. Notifications off outside them.
Financial models are deep work. Do them before the market opens, never in gaps between messages.
Hard-stop at 7pm on weekdays. The constraint is what forces the triage.

speaking.drill: Ask yourself an interview question, answer it, and physically close your mouth. Count three seconds before adding anything.

interview_tech.q: Walk me through how a $1M inventory write-down flows through all three statements.
interview_tech.a: P&L: COGS up $1M, so gross profit, EBIT and pre-tax income each fall $1M. At a 25% rate, net income falls $750K. Cash flow: start from net income −$750K, add back the $1M non-cash write-down, so operating cash flow rises $250K — the tax shield. Balance sheet: inventory −$1M, cash +$250K, so assets fall $750K; retained earnings fall $750K. It balances. The point they are testing: you know the write-down is non-cash and that the only real cash effect is tax.

interview_tech.q: How do you value a new store before signing a 10-year lease?
interview_tech.a: Build an unlevered free cash flow model over the lease term. Revenue from catchment population, comparable sales density and a ramp curve — never assume year-one maturity. Deduct COGS, rent with escalation clauses, staff, and allocated overhead only if genuinely incremental. Capex is fit-out plus initial inventory. Discount at WACC and test IRR versus hurdle, payback, and NPV. Then sensitise the two variables that actually decide it: year-one sales and the ramp. A store that only clears the hurdle at 100% of forecast is a no.

interview_soft.q: How would your team describe your management style?
interview_soft.a: Answer with evidence rather than adjectives. 'They would say I am specific — I give the number I expect and the date, and I do not change it quietly. They would also say I go into detail on their work more than some managers, which is useful when they are learning and irritating when they are not, so I have had to learn where to stop.' Naming the downside of your own style is what makes the strength believable.

interview_soft.q: How do you handle stress and long hours during close or audit?
interview_soft.a: They are checking sustainability, not stoicism. Do not claim you thrive on pressure. Give the operating answer: what you do to make the peak smaller (moving work out of the close), how you protect the team (rotating the worst shifts, protecting recovery time after), and what you personally do that is non-negotiable. Having a young child is relevant here and worth saying — it reads as someone with real boundaries rather than someone who has not been tested yet.

cfo_field.q: Explain a variance in one sentence or you do not understand it yet.
cfo_field.a: 'Margin is down 180bps: 120 from promotional depth in electronics, 40 from freight, 20 mix.' That is a CFO answer. A table of forty lines is a controller answer. The discipline is to decompose until the drivers are additive and then name the largest two. If you cannot make the bridge add up, you have a data problem, not a communication problem.

cfo_field.q: Working capital is where a retail CFO is actually judged.
cfo_field.a: EBITDA gets the headline; the cash conversion cycle gets the board's attention. DIO + DSO − DPO. Retail is inventory-heavy and often near-zero DSO, so the fight is DIO against DPO. Cutting DIO from 95 to 80 days on AED 400M COGS releases roughly AED 16.4M of cash — permanently, without selling a single extra unit. That is a bigger number than most cost programmes deliver, and it does not need a headcount conversation.

lichess_summary.session_summary: Your 64 % win rate looks respectable on paper, but it masks a dangerous reliance on a single, low‑quality opening repertoire—four games of Philidor (C41) and you’re only 2‑2, a 50 % return that any 1500‑rated opponent will exploit. Drop the Philidor entirely, replace it with a solid, theory‑tested line like the Classical French or the Caro‑Kann, and drill the resulting pawn structures until they become second nature. From now on, every week schedule two “opening‑only” training sessions where you play 10 rapid games exclusively with your new lines, review each game move by move, and eliminate any lingering Philidor habits before your next tournament.
